articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: When Emmanuel Macron came to power in 2017 , at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu , who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire , including the 19 th -century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews . The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

articles.title: Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.

articles.title: A greying population, a strained care system
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Girija (name changed) spent years working as a domestic worker before her failing knees made it difficult for her to continue. Hoping to find a more manageable way to earn a living, the 60-year-old borrowed money from acquaintances and set up a roadside vegetable stall. But another health problem emerged, making it difficult to keep the business running.

“She learnt that she was suffering from urinary incontinence. Taking frequent loo breaks while managing the stall was not practical, and she eventually decided to shut shop, losing her source of income in the process,” says Gurajada Sobha Pernidevi, founder-president of Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, a voluntary organisation working for the welfare of women.

For older people with limited financial means, a health problem can do more than cause physical discomfort; it can take away their livelihood, independence and opportunities to socialise. Conditions that are difficult to discuss, such as urinary incontinence, are often endured in silence because of embarrassment and the cost of managing them.

Unlike ailments that call for joint replacement surgery or a cardiac stent, these less visible difficulties of ageing often receive scant attention, despite their potential to disrupt daily life. However, as Telangana’s share of elderly population grows, addressing such overlooked needs will become increasingly important.

Telangana’s population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 12.5% in 2026 to 17.1% in 2036, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s report, ‘State Finances — A Study of Budgets of 2025-26: Demographic Transition in India — Implications for State Finances’.

The State is expected to join the category of ageing ones, where senior citizens account for at least 15% of the population. The projected demographic shift raises questions about how healthcare, caregiving and community support can keep pace with the needs of older people, particularly those who live alone or cannot afford private services.
Associations working with senior citizens say the challenges range from obtaining medicines and reaching hospitals to finding dependable caregivers and accessing mental health support.

P. Shyam Kumar, State project coordinator at HelpAge India, says doorstep medical services, including palliative care, could make healthcare more accessible. Nutritional supplements and the delivery of medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists could also help older people manage their health.

“Without adequate support, their condition may deteriorate, leading to more hospital visits, additional expenses and greater dependence on family members. So, supplying medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists may work in this direction,” he adds.

Access to healthcare is not simply a matter of getting an appointment or obtaining medicines. Older people who depend on younger family members for hospital visits may have to wait until someone can take time off work and accompany them.

Members of several associations say a family member’s availability often influences whether and when an older person seeks medical attention. Those with limited mobility may need transport, a wheelchair or stretcher. In a multi-storey building without a suitable lift, even getting someone downstairs can require additional assistance and planning. Hospital visits can involve long walks between departments, diagnostic tests and consultations, making them particularly difficult for those without someone to accompany them.

The problem does not end at the hospital gate. For older people who cannot leave home, finding a doctor willing to make a home visit can be equally difficult. “This is a crucial requirement of those who are unable to step out of their house,” says Sobha.

articles.title: Southern States should strengthen intelligence-sharing, operational coordination: Telangana CM
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Calling for a united front against criminal networks operating across State borders, Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy on Friday (October 23, 2026) urged southern States to strengthen intelligence-sharing and operational coordination, stressing that no State could effectively combat crime in isolation.

Inaugurating the Southern States’ Police Coordination Committee meeting at the Telangana Integrated Command and Control Centre (TGICCC) in Hyderabad, the Chief Minister offered to share Telangana’s technological infrastructure and policing practices with neighbouring States to tackle cybercrime, narcotics trafficking and organised crime.

The meeting brought together senior police officials from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala, besides representatives from the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Puducherry and Lakshadweep, and central investigating and security agencies.

“It is your responsibility to make South India safer and bring crime to the lowest possible levels by developing strong mechanisms for cross-border coordination between police headquarters,” the Chief Minister said at the gathering.

He urged the participating police chiefs to formulate a comprehensive action plan to improve coordination between police headquarters, emphasising that emerging challenges such as cybercrime, narcotics and traffic management required specialised training, technology and cooperation.

Highlighting Telangana’s policing reforms, the Chief Minister said the State had secured the top position in tackling cybercrime during the Prime Minister’s PRAGATI review, while the E lite Action Group for Drug Law Enforcement (EAGLE) had scored over 80% in the Union government’s assessment of anti-narcotics efforts.

He said Union Home Minister Amit Shah had congratulated Telangana police officers for making the State completely free of Naxal violence. The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau had also established new standards in recovering money lost by victims of cyber fraud.

The Chief Minister highlighted the establishment of specialised agencies, including EAGLE, HYDRAA and TG-SAFE, to address emerging challenges. While HYDRAA protected and rejuvenated lakes and other water bodies besides safeguarding public properties, TG-SAFE was established on the lines of the United States Food and Drug Administration to strengthen food and drug regulation.

He also referred to the recruitment of transgender persons as Traffic Assistants in Hyderabad, describing it as a first-of-its-kind initiative in the country, and highlighted the administrative benefits of dividing policing responsibilities among the Hyderabad, Cyberabad and Malkajgiri Police Commissionerates.

On police welfare, he said the government had established the Young India Police School to provide quality education to children of police personnel — from Home Guards to the Director General of Police — with standards comparable to leading Sainik Schools.

The government had also enhanced ex-gratia compensation for police personnel killed in the line of duty to between ₹1 crore and ₹2 crore, depending on rank, besides providing housing plots to bereaved families and compassionate appointments to eligible family members.

Maintaining that efficient, ethical and impartial policing was the first expectation of citizens, the Chief Minister said resources allocated to police modernisation and welfare should be viewed as an investment in public safety rather than expenditure.

articles.title: Brisk polling in eight Bihar MLC seats; 150 candidates in fray
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The biennial election to eight Bihar Legislative Council seats witnessed brisk polling in the first two hours on Friday (October 23, 2026), with the Saran Teachers’ constituency recording the highest turnout at 13.56%, followed by Patna at 12.88%.

As many as 5.32 lakh voters were eligible to decide the fate of 150 candidates in the fray. According to the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, among the Graduates’ constituencies, Darbhanga recorded the highest turnout at 8%, followed by Patna at 5.5%, Kosi at 5.14% and Tirhut at 4.81%.

Among the Teachers’ constituencies, Saran recorded the highest turnout, followed by Patna, then Darbhanga at 12% and Tirhut at 5.88%. The average voting percentage for the Graduates’ constituencies was 5.86%, and for the Teachers’, 11.08%.

Voting began at 8 a.m. and will continue until 4 p.m. The combined electorate stands at 5,32,847, including 1,46,611 women and 37 third-gender voters, across 933 polling stations. Counting of votes will take place on October 27, 2026. “Polling has so far been peaceful,” an official said.

The contest in the Patna Graduates constituency has drawn the most attention, following a rift within the JD(U), with Mokama MLA Anant Singh backing Jan Suraaj Party candidate Anuj Singh against his own party’s nominee, Neeraj Kumar.

Mr. Kumar, a former Minister and a close aide of former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar, is seeking a fourth consecutive term from the seat. Mr. Singh has extended support to Mr. Anuj Singh, alleging that Neeraj Kumar had worked against him during last year’s Assembly elections.

“People are the real masters. It is for them to decide the fate of candidates. I am confident that Anuj Singh will win the election with a massive mandate,” Mr. Singh told reporters. On Nitish Kumar’s brief meeting with Neeraj Kumar on Thursday (October 22, 2026), Mr. Singh said the JD(U) chief “goes wherever they take him.”
Mr. Singh, along with Jan Suraaj founder Prashant Kishor, has been regularly claiming that JD(U) candidate Neeraj Kumar does not have the support of the party chief.
Meanwhile, JD(U) leader Shyam Rajak, whose party is a major constituent of the ruling alliance, said voting was continuing smoothly and that there was a wave of support for the NDA.

Apart from Patna Graduates, the other constituencies where polling is under way are Darbhanga Graduates, Tirhut Graduates, Kosi Graduates, Patna Teachers, Darbhanga Teachers, Tirhut Teachers and Saran Teachers.

One of the early voters in the Patna Teachers’ constituency, Murli Manohar Srivastava, told PTI Videos: “The biggest issue this time is that of teachers working in unaided schools who do not receive proper government financial assistance. Our long-standing demand has been for a formal pay scale, pension and social security. We have been making sustained and strong appeals for it to be fulfilled.”

The 1981 Non-Funded Education Policy was modified by the Nitish Kumar-led government in 2008 to usher in a performance-based grant system. Under it, the Bihar government provides post-result grants to private or community-run educational institutions that largely sustain themselves on students’ fees; the staff there do not have a regular pay scale, leading to unstable income.

articles.title: Economics beyond the individual
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford’s work modelling the macroeconomy based on individual agents’ decisions has significant implications for monetary policy. Despite being hailed as providing a rigorous foundation for stabilisation policies, focusing on the individual blinds us to the way the macroeconomy actually works. It may seem paradoxical; John Maynard Keynes’s insight was that the aggregate economy cannot be understood simply as the sum of individual actions. Heterodox economics, by focusing on the structure of the broader economy rather than its individual components, provides a much better framework for understanding the economy.
The work of Keynes in the wake of the Great Depression led to the development of the study of the aggregate economy, as opposed to studying demand and supply of individual commodities.
Microeconomics focuses on the optimising behaviour of the individual, while macroeconomics focuses on statistical relationships to characterise aggregate behaviour.

Hall and Woodford provided rigorous models that rooted the study of macroeconomic aggregates, such as consumption, investment and employment, in the behaviour of individual agents. A key contribution was linking consumption to interest rates and the future. Individuals chose to smooth consumption over their lifetimes rather than base it solely on their current needs.

When interest rates were high, savings yielded greater returns. Individuals therefore had an incentive to defer some consumption to earn more and consume more in the future. Higher interest rates could reduce current consumption and hence lower current demand, and vice versa. Macroeconomic dynamics could consequently be derived from rigorous formulations of how individuals responded to market signals and policy variables such as interest rates.

This provided a framework within which Central Bankers could target an interest rate that was ‘neutral’ to the real economy — one that neither excessively stimulated nor depressed aggregate demand — greatly aiding the development of sophisticated stabilisation paradigms for monetary policy.

However, this approach collapsed the distinction between consumption, savings and investment. By viewing consumption inter-temporally, and by making it the main component of demand, the microfoundations methodology relegated the importance of volatile investment expectations to the background. Whatever was not consumed currently was saved, and automatically translated into future consumption demand. This was the framework followed by classical economics, which Keynes contested. He cautioned that not all saving is necessarily undertaken for future consumption.

In contrast, investment is fuelled by expectations of business owners as to prospects of profit. There is no necessity for the savings behaviour of individuals to always imply a demand for future consumption, and hence investment, by businesses. How can businesses determine whether an act of individual savings is to spend on a house for the future, or to ward against a future health emergency that may or may not occur? In such a situation, the interest rate cannot serve as an indicator of the extent of future consumption.
Keynes further suggested a radical intervention. It was not the interest rate that equated savings and investment, but income. Investment raised income, and generated an equal amount of savings.

This is not merely a technical insight, but an important way in which to view policy. It is not savings or inter-temporal consumption demand that affects output growth and employment, but business investment. To understand why economies are prone to instability, one must examine the investment behaviour of companies rather than the consumption demands of individuals.

According to Keynes, investment being done for profit in an environment of uncertainty is the chief source of economic instability. In uncertain situations, it is rational for investors to follow the herd, investing during a boom for fear of missing out on speculative returns, and withdrawing investment in a recession for fear of loss. This is the reason why booms and recessions get amplified. The work of Keynesians such as Hyman Minsky and Jan Kregel offers great insight into how the financial behaviour of firms brought about the boom in housing construction and finance, as well as the recession in 2008. Much of the current stock market gains in the U.S. economy are being driven by AI hyperscalers, giving rise to concerns of a new bubble that might eventually burst. Such outcomes can be clearly discerned when viewed from a Keynesian lens.

Some might argue that it does not matter how one views the economy, if the framework designed to bring about stability is effective. Moreover, in centering the actions of individuals, so the argument goes, this framework takes into account the reality of a complex economy being driven by individual choices.

articles.title: Why managing fiscal is a tightrope for State governments
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are among the most socially and economically advanced States in India. Yet, the finances of both governments, like those of most other States, are under stress. The White Papers recently released by the two governments described their outstanding debt as alarming. State government debt is often vilified as the result of fiscal mismanagement. But it may, in fact, reflect a mismatch between development aspirations and the limited fiscal capacity of State governments.

Debts build up over the years with deficits, which arise when the government’s expenditure overshoots its tax and other receipts. In India, while the power to raise taxes rests largely with the Union government, a larger share of overall government spending is borne by the State governments. A majority of the State government expenditure is on social sectors, such as health and education, and economic sectors, such as agriculture and irrigation, all of which have a direct impact on people’s lives and livelihoods. In Kerala, the high levels of State government spending on social sectors since the 1960s have been a central constituent of the public action driving social progress. Compared with the corresponding average for all Indian States, per capita State government social expenditure was higher in Kerala and Tamil Nadu (by 30% and 20%, respectively). In contrast, it was markedly lower in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (by 35% and 40%) (for the period 2020-23, according to an analysis based on State Finances: A Study of Budgets, Reserve Bank of India).

articles.title: The reality behind falling net FDI
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: I ndia’s net foreign direct investment (FDI) has declined drastically in recent years. Critics see the weak net flows as a sign of weakness, while the Chief Economic Adviser points to the large inflows and rising manufacturing FDI as evidence of strength. He links weak net flows to profit repatriation and outward investment by Indian companies.

However, this debate overlooks a major issue. By focusing on overall numbers, both sides ignore the changing composition of international capital and the Balance of Payments (BoP) mechanisms that govern inflows and outflows.

For BoP purposes, net FDI is calculated as the difference between inflows and outflows after adjusting for the repatriation of capital. From the peak of $44.0 billion in 2020-21, net FDI fell to less than $1 billion in 2024-25. It recovered to $7.6 billion in 2025-26. The corresponding gross inflow was $94.6 billion.

It is necessary to note that India’s liberal FDI policy, introduced in 1991, initially emphasised technology acquisition, export promotion, and foreign exchange conservation. Over time, policy increasingly prioritised attracting larger inflows, while concerns regarding future external payment obligations and investment quality receded.

FDI is often viewed as a uniform, long-term commitment that brings technology and management skills to the host country. FDI can fall into three different investor classes, each with distinct capabilities, strategies, and exit timelines.

The first category is real FDI (RFDI), consisting of traditional multinational enterprises with the technology, brands, and capabilities to establish production and services. These generally represent long-term commitments.

The second category comprises financial investors, including private equity funds, venture capital firms, sovereign wealth funds, and asset managers. Their main goal is capital growth and planned exits.

The third category includes diaspora investments and special purpose vehicles (SPVs). These involve capital raised abroad and funneled through offshore financial centres, sometimes including the round-tripping of Indian funds.

Data on remittance-level FDI from the past four years, from 2022-23 to 2025-26 up to December, show that RFDI made up 41.9% of “effective inflows.” Financial investors followed closely with a 40.5% share, while the remaining 17.6% came from the diaspora and SPVs linked to India.

The business model of financial investors suggests future exits that result in large-scale capital repatriations. A notable example occurred in 2025 when Singapore’s Temasek exited Schneider Electric India Ltd., earning $6.4 billion on an investment of $637 million made in 2020. Total recorded divestment in CY 2025 was $52 billion, with 45 major foreign private equity and venture capital exits accounting for $29 billion in outflows.

Based on an analysis of effective inflows, FDI in India’s manufacturing sector has declined across three consecutive four-year periods. Most notably, RFDI into manufacturing accounted for only 10.6% of total effective inflows during the most recent four-year period.

A major blind spot in gross FDI figures is the mixing of new capital injections with corporate accounting changes, such as intra-group ownership reorganisations, mergers, share swaps, and the conversion of earlier non-equity instruments such as external commercial borrowings (ECBs) and convertible debentures.

From the peak of $44.0 billion in 2020-21, net FDI fell to less than $1 billion in 2024-25. It recovered to $7.6 billion in 2025-26. The corresponding gross inflow was $94.6 billion.

articles.title: SBI’s cyber defences: What the bank had in place
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The suspected customer-data exposure at State Bank of India (SBI) has brought its cybersecurity preparedness into focus, despite the bank reporting an extensive array of safeguards in its annual disclosures.

SBI’s FY2025–26 Sustainability Report and Annual Report, published before the reported exposure, detail its security audits, automated threat monitoring, incident-response procedures and employee training. The disclosures also outline plans to further integrate its cyber-defence operations.

SBI’s Sustainability Report says information-systems audits covered 427 IT systems during FY26. Audits of outsourced IT activities covered 695 activities, while internal and external cybersecurity audits covered 176 IT applications and infrastructure and 151 systems, respectively.
However, the report does not disclose the findings, the number of vulnerabilities identified or how many were rectified. SBI reported “nil” instances of data breaches during FY26.

The bank’s Global Cyber Security Operations Centre (GCSOC) continuously monitors critical information systems for threats and unauthorised access. Automated tracking of indicators of compromise (IoCs)—digital clues that may signal cyberattacks—has replaced a previously manual process.
SBI also monitors phishing, fraudulent websites, brand impersonation, vishing and rogue mobile applications, pursuing the removal of malicious links and websites.

Its Annual Report cites an automated Secure Configuration Monitoring System covering more than 85,000 IT assets. AI-driven intelligence platforms, risk profiling and continuous monitoring of digital transactions help identify suspicious activity.

Security testing includes ethical hacking, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and red-team exercises across websites, mobile applications, databases, networks and internal systems. Monthly domain-password-spray tests seek to identify employees using easily guessed passwords.
Firewalls, encryption, multi-factor authentication and data-loss prevention tools provide additional safeguards.

CERT SBI serves as the central first responder to cyber incidents. Its response framework covers detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident reviews. A separate Incident Response Wing handles forensic investigations, threat hunting, mock drills and regulatory reporting.

SBI conducted 2,079 information-security and cybersecurity training programmes, benefiting 39,961 employees in FY26. Nearly 1.81 lakh employees had completed mandatory cybersecurity e-learning and assessments by March 31, 2026.
Oversight rests with the Board-level IT Strategy Committee, while the Group Chief Information Security Officer heads the Information Security Department.

Iran-backed Houthi forces targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Thursday, while Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted an attempted drone attack near Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil facility.
In a statement, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said the intercepted attack occurred outside the facility’s perimeter and did not affect operations.

The incident reportedly claimed two lives and injured two people, including an Indian national. The airport attack also killed two people, including an Indian national, while another two Indian nationals were injured

articles.title: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding , following the devastating floods in August.

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022, and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.
The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

articles.title: Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Most of the immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud had applied for U.S. citizenship and now face charges related to lying on forms or during interviews. Those charges could lead to years in prison and thwart their efforts to naturalise.
Amandeep Kaur, who is among those charged, has lived in the country for eight years and is in the process of becoming a naturalised U.S. citizen, said her husband, Kulwinder Singh.

Mr. Singh said she got her driver's license in 2024 but took the written test at the DMV in Hindi because she struggles with English. He doesn't know if she registered to vote then. He said she received and returned a ballot in 2024 but they both thought it was a registration form.
Now, he said his wife is distraught with the news that she may have done something illegal.
“All she does is cry. It's heartbreaking,” said Mr. Singh, who is a U.S. citizen.

One of them is José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, who applied for citizenship in October 2025 after living in the country for 40 years and spending his entire adult life as a legal permanent resident. The federal government has alleged in charging documents that he improperly claimed to be a citizen in 2007 when registering to vote, then later lied about it on his immigration paperwork. The government hasn't accused him of casting a ballot.

Bañuelos-Díaz told The Associated Press he had no idea he had registered to vote until he was arrested on Monday (October 19, 2026) outside his Los Angeles home, though he recalls getting a driver's license around 2007. In California, people are prompted to register to vote when applying for a driver's license.
“I have never voted because I know I can't vote,” he said. “If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later.”
He was released from custody after his arrest but faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

Federal authorities on Monday (October 19, 2026) charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents in California in a crackdown on people accused of illegally voting or registering to do so. As of Thursday (October 22, 2026) morning, the government had filed charging documents in 10 of the 28 cases, offering additional details about how authorities relied on voter registration data to pursue broader criminal charges around immigration status.

Most of the immigrants charged in California have lived in the country for at least five years, and some of them for decades. They could face deportation if they lied on their citizenship application.
Immigrants convicted of illegally voting in the United States face up to a year in prison. Those convicted of lying on applications to become American citizens face up to a decade.

Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping has ordered all-out search and rescue efforts for the missing and prompt medical treatment for the injured affected by the quake.
Mr. Xi made the remarks in his instruction, calling for every effort to minimise casualties.

The number of people injured in a magnitude 7 earthquake that struck Tibet has ‌risen to 65, local government said in a social media post on ⁠Friday (October 23), while the death count remained unchanged at 16.

More than 300 police ‌officers ⁠including traffic and community police personnel ⁠were sent to the epicentre to carry out rescue and emergency relief work, the Nagqu police department said in a separate ‌post on messaging app WeChat early on Friday.
Officers sent to the region checked for damage to homes and helped people relocate to ‌safer locations, the Nagqu police also said in the WeChat post.
As per Xinhua , at least 339 houses have collapsed, while the full extent of the damage is still being assessed. A rescue team has been sent to the affected area.
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that railway authorities have suspended train services through the earthquake-hit areas.
The National Centre for Seismology (NCS) on X stated, “The quake occurred at 20:03:43 IST at a depth of 173 km, with its epicentre at latitude 32.368 N and longitude 93.853 E, according to the NCS.”
Search and rescue efforts continued following the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,000 tents and folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.

articles.title: What is Romanch’s Law? New York City’s historic horse carriage ban after Indian tourist’s death
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: In a significant move to end a longstanding tradition, the New York City Council voted on Thursday (October 22, 2026) to pass legislation banning horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park. The bill, known as Romanch’s Law, ends the historic tourist attraction after decades of debate over animal welfare and public safety. The bill is named after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, who died following a carriage accident in Central Park earlier this year.

Of ​the city's 51 lawmakers, 40 supported the bill, backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who had earlier this month said the horse-drawn carriage industry would end. ‌Seven council members voted against it and two abstained.

Romanch’s Law is a landmark municipal legislation that phases out the horse-drawn carriage industry in New York City by June 1, 2028. First introduced by Council Member Christopher Marte and championed by Council Speaker Julie Menin, the law prohibits operation of horse-drawn cabs while providing a transition plan for affected workers and humane protections for retired horses.

The transition program includes job referrals, career counselling, hiring fairs and financial compensation for business owners. The law includes strict animal welfare safeguards requiring horse owners to certify by June 1, 2027, that no retired horses will be sold or transferred for slaughter or any inhumane purpose..

Although efforts to ban or reform carriage rides date back to 2007, it reached a tipping point following a fatal accident in Central Park on June 17, 2026, when the Indian tourist Romanch Mahajan lost his life during a family trip when a carriage horse bolted after the driver stepped out to take a photograph.

As the horse panicked, Romanch’s mother fell from the vehicle and Romanch jumped out to assist her, sustaining fatal injuries. The tragedy led Speaker Julie Menin to convene city council hearing in July 2026 and Council Member Marte subsequently renamed his legislative effort, previously called Ryder’s Law to Romanch’s Law in honour of the teenager's memory.

The ban drew mixed reactions from across political and advocacy groups. Speaker Julie Menin and animal rights organisations such as PETA and NYCLASS celebrated the vote as a victory for public safety and animal welfare, with PETA offering fifty thousand dollars to assist with retiring the horses to rescue farms.

Meanwhile, the Transport Workers Union, representing carriage owners and drivers, announced plans to seek temporary restraining orders in court, with their stance being that the law deprives business owners of their livelihood.
Medet Fidan, a former cab driver who traded his steering wheel for a set of reins after ride-sharing apps upended the taxi industry, said he felt like he was being targeted.

“I think the city is leaving us a big mess,” said Fidan, 56, who has been driving a carriage for 15 years. “We’re going to lose our businesses, we’re going to lose our jobs, we’re going to lose our livelihoods.”
President Donald Trump also expressed scepticism on Truth Social, questioning why carriages were banned while cars remain permitted.

The bill requires the city ‌to develop a transition plan for the workforce by April and to consider a program to compensate carriage operators for their businesses and help with the disposition of their horses. Under the proposal, the horses could not be slaughtered.

articles.title: Trump says Starshield restored in Ukraine, declines to say if he contacted Musk
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The Starshield military communications system is "back" in Ukraine, Donald Trump said on Thursday (October 22, 2026), after the Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. President asked tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore the service, which is vital to Kyiv's forces.
"I don't want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether somebody else called — doesn't make any difference," Mr. Trump told journalists when asked about the report.
"I guess the bottom line, he put it back," Mr. Trump said, referring to Mr. Musk.
The Journal reported earlier this week that Mr. Musk had capped the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the system, making some of Kyiv's drones useless.

Mr. Musk had previously said that "any limits on speed or usage" of Starshield systems — which are operated by his SpaceX company — were "decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS," referring to Mr. Trump.
But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday (October 20, 2026) that the Pentagon had not directed any changes to Starshield, and Mr. Trump said last week he did not do so either.

Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink's military-grade satellite service, for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russia-occupied territory, and its interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX's parallel Starlink civilian satellite system.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have been increasingly tense in recent days, with Mr. Trump calling for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced after he criticised a U.S. deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

articles.title: Shamonda virus, the livestock pathogen detected in human for the first time | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: France reported the first known human infection with Shamonda virus on October 22, 2026. The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, died in early October. Investigations are underway to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the death, and how the patient acquired the infection.

French authorities suspect that the patient was infected by the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during spring and summer. The specific insect responsible has not been identified. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey.

French authorities say that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also said that wider spread is unlikely based on the information currently available. However, investigations into the human case are continuing.

Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae . It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus.

The virus was first isolated from cattle in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in parts of Africa and Japan. Before the recent case in France, it was considered an animal pathogen that did not infect humans.

Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although infections have also been detected in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. In livestock, infection can cause fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, loss of appetite and reduced milk production. In pregnant animals, it has been associated with abortions and congenital abnormalities in offspring.

Neurological signs have also been reported in horses infected with the virus in Europe. The extent to which the variants circulating in Europe differ in their effects on animal health remains under investigation.

The virus is understood to spread primarily through the bites of infected Culicoides midges, tiny blood-feeding insects. The precise midge species responsible for transmitting the European variants has not yet been established.

According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), there is currently no evidence of horizontal transmission, or spread between animals through direct contact or other routes. Vertical transmission, from a pregnant animal to its offspring, has been reported.

Two genetically distinct variants, designated Shamonda virus Europe 1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe 2 (SHAV-EU2), have been identified in Europe in 2026. Research indicates that they may have been introduced separately. Their geographical distribution, effects on livestock and long-term significance remain under investigation.

The detection in a human has raised questions about whether Shamonda virus can cause disease beyond its known animal hosts. French authorities have reported that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were considered very likely to be linked to the infection. However, investigations are continuing to establish whether the virus caused or contributed to the death.

The patient was severely immunocompromised and had an underlying serious illness. It is not yet known whether similar complications would occur in people with different health conditions or whether people without immune suppression could develop symptomatic infection.

articles.title: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding , following the devastating floods in August.

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022, and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.
The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

articles.title: Fitbit Air Review | Screenless companion for easy health monitoring
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: I remember Fitbit as a slim tracking device worn on the wrist , from a time when fitness bands were about counting steps and monitoring activity, long before the smartwatch craze took over. Over the years, wearables have evolved into mini smartphones, complete with displays, notifications and apps.

With the Fitbit Air, Google brings back some of that original simplicity in a new avatar. Priced at ₹13,999 in India, this screenless tracker focuses on health monitoring, sleep insights and activity tracking, with Google Health and Gemini-powered coaching adding a layer of intelligence. It is designed to stay out of the way while keeping tabs on your health throughout the day.
After spending time with it, the question is whether this return to the basics works for today’s fitness-focused users. Let’s find out.

The Fitbit Air takes a different approach to wearable design by keeping the hardware compact and unobtrusive. The tracking module weighs just 5.2 grams, while the device weighs around 12 grams with its band. It has a small, pebble-shaped sensor housed inside a woven fabric strap, giving it the appearance of a simple wristband rather than a conventional smartwatch. There is no display or physical button, which keeps the design clean and minimal.

Comfort is one of the Fitbit Air’s biggest strengths. Its lightweight construction makes it comfortable to wear throughout the day and while sleeping. The woven band sits gently on the wrist, while its adjustable fastening helps achieve a secure fit for continuous tracking. This matters for a device designed to collect health data around the clock, rather than something you wear only during workouts. The tracker also has a detachable sensor module, allowing you to change bands without replacing the device.

The Fitbit Air has a small status LED that responds to a firm double-tap. A white light indicates sufficient battery, while red signals that the charge is low. It also includes a vibration motor for silent alarms and reminders. The tracker offers water resistance up to 50 metres, making it suitable for swimming, although the fabric band needs proper drying after water exposure. Google offers the tracker in Obsidian, Berry, Lavender and Fog, with interchangeable band options.

The Fitbit Air relies on the Google Health app for almost everything beyond collecting data. Once paired with a smartphone, it tracks activity and health metrics in the background and syncs them to the app. The dashboard brings together steps, sleep, heart rate, readiness and cardio load, making it possible to review daily activity without needing a screen on the wrist.

The app offers plenty of information, although understanding some of the metrics takes time. Its separate sections for Today, Fitness, Sleep and Health make it easier to explore individual readings. You can also connect supported health services and devices. Another useful feature is the ability to keep the Fitbit Air and a Pixel Watch connected to the same account. This works well if you prefer a smartwatch during the day but want a lighter tracker for sleeping.

Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini, is one of the more interesting additions. Available through a Google Health Premium subscription, it interprets health data, suggests workouts, explains recovery scores and helps create personalised fitness plans. Instead of simply presenting numbers, it aims to explain what they mean and how you can act on them. However, some recommendations can feel generic, and the feature needs refinement before its guidance consistently feels personal. It should also be treated as a wellness tool, and not a substitute for medical advice.

Google includes a three-month Premium trial with the Fitbit Air. After that, the subscription costs ₹499 per month or ₹4,999 annually. Basic activity tracking, sleep information and several recovery metrics remain available without a subscription, which means you can continue using the core features without an ongoing payment.

The Fitbit Air’s screenless design makes the experience genuinely distraction-free. You do not have notifications appearing on your wrist or a display encouraging you to check it repeatedly. The tracker collects information quietly, leaving the phone app to handle the analysis. This approach works particularly well for people who want to monitor their health without adding another source of digital interruptions.

Sleep tracking is one of the more detailed parts of the experience. The Fitbit Air automatically detects sleep and daytime naps, so you do not have to start a session manually. During testing, it recorded sleep duration and estimated the time spent in deep, REM and light sleep. It also highlighted periods of restlessness and time spent awake. The presentation makes it easy to see how the night unfolded, although sleep stages remain estimates rather than clinical measurements.

articles.title: Inadequate sleep increases the risk of fatty liver disease
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: In 2018, anatomists at the Toho University Graduate School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan, performed a sleep deprivation experiment on lab mice. Mice usually sleep for 12 hours a day. In this experiment, researchers induced sleep deprivation using the ‘gentle handling method’ during sleep hours so that the mice could sleep only for six hours daily.

They discovered that liver fat content in sleep-deprived mice increased without total weight gain compared to another group who were allowed to sleep normally. The liver cells were stressed, and the activity of certain genes that escalate insulin resistance and fat content within liver cells also increased with sleep deprivation.

Three years later, a group of Chinese researchers at the Xinjiang Medical University went one step ahead. In this experiment, rats were severely sleep-deprived, turning into insomniacs. Liver enzymes, blood, and liver fat increased substantially. None of these changes were notable among rats who were allowed to sleep without distractions.

They also found the reason for increased liver fat in insomniac mice — the sympathetic nerves that supplied the liver, best known for their role in responding to stress and danger, were hyperactive. When insomnia was treated with a sleeping pill in these stressed rats, the liver fat was reduced with adequate sleep.

There are lessons here, of mice and men. Sleep is an underrated activity among humans. Sometimes, the intentional and forced lack of sleep ‘to increase productivity’ is advertised by men in power to showcase their self-proclaimed metahuman nature. During an interview in 2011, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he had become a workaholic and hardly slept for 3.5 hours in a day, and that yoga and pranayama routine kept him energised and awake.

But medical science has a different story to tell. A study of nearly 55,500 people from Europe showed that those who slept 7-8.5 hours daily had higher life expectancy than those who slept less than seven hours. In those between ages 50 and 75 without sleep disturbances, the expectation of living longer without chronic disease development was significantly higher.
And yoga interventions improved overall sleep quality, efficiency, latency, and duration, contrary to all claims.

Sleep is a vital function of human life and accounts for up to one-third of the lifespan. Contrary to normal belief, during sleep, the brain is not ‘resting’ but is engaged in various activities necessary to improve well-being, increase life, and especially impact the liver. The minimum required duration for ‘healthy’ sleep is seven hours.

When 10,000 persons with sleep disorders were followed up for one year, incident fatty liver disease was noted in 14, while in those without sleep disorders, it was only six. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease association was significantly higher among persons with shorter sleep duration (less than six hours per night) and excessive daytime sleepiness. A high-quality study showed that inadequate sleep duration was strongly associated with an elevated risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and adequate sleep helped prevent it. With every one-hour decrease in sleep time from the recommended seven-eight hours, the risk of fat deposition in the liver increased by 24% compared with those who slept adequately.

However, when people who lost sleep during the weekdays caught up on the debt during weekends (known as weekend catch-up sleep), the development of fatty liver disease reduced significantly. Compared with non-nappers, long daytime nappers (more than 60 minutes) had a higher risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Correlation may not be causation, but with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is associated with other conditions such as obesity, high blood pressure, increased waist-hip ratio, low functioning thyroid, and high blood cholesterol, studying and identifying independent associations make realistic sense.

In people who sleep less than six hours at night, have a persistently poor sleep quality, or nap more than one hour during the day, independent of other disease conditions, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease development was a strong association. The next time someone brags that sacrificing time and quality of sleep is an achievement associated with success, know that success comes with fatty liver disease. And it is not worth it.

articles.title: India’s smartphone shipments collapsed to a decade low during Q3 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: India’s smartphone shipments fell to a decade low by 20% year-over-year (YoY) during Q3 2026, noted Counterpoint Research. This steep fall during the July-September period was mainly due to high memory prices that led to constant increase in smartphone costs which resulted in softer demand, as OEMs held inventories.

“Rising component costs pushed device prices higher, putting increasing pressure on affordability and weakening the traditional mass-market volume engine, particularly below ₹15,000,” said Research Analyst Shubham Singh. “Sub-₹20,000 shipments declined by 47% in Q3 2026 as rising model prices pushed devices into higher price bands,” he added.
During Q3, 2026, Samsung became the top smartphone brand in India, after nine quarters, with a 17% share. The Galaxy A series drove volumes, the research firm said.
Vivo came second with a 16% share as their Y series continued to drive volumes. Oppo was at third position with a 12% market share. Xiaomi ranked fourth with a 12% share.

Counterpoint said that Apple iPhone 18 Pro series seen a strong start in India, with initial sales nearly 20% higher YoY than those of the iPhone 17 Pro series. It also mentioned that there’s a continued demand for the iPhone 17 lineup even after Apple pricing adjustments across its portfolio.
MediaTek was the top chipset OEM with a 45% share in Q3 2026 in India.

“We expect India’s smartphone market to shrink by around 13% in 2026, with continued pricing pressure weighing on affordability and replacement demand. The post-festive seasonal slowdown will add to the pressure, while elevated component costs are likely to drive another round of price hikes after the festive season sale,” said Research Director Tarun Pathak.

articles.title: Explained: What do the National Medical Commission’s new guidelines say about advertising in medicine?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: On October 6, the National Medical Commission (NMC) issued guidelines on advertising and public communication by doctors and hospitals. Intended to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, they cover hospital hoardings, social media and artificial intelligence (AI). Beyond curbing deception, they raise another question regarding how much can doctors and hospitals say to the public about their work and achievements?

Claims of “guaranteed cures”, “100% success” or being the “best” are barred. Similarly, fake reviews, manipulated online rankings, misleading celebrity or influencer endorsements, and offers encouraging unnecessary treatment are deemed unethical practices. The guidelines rightfully prohibit AI-generated or manipulated patient images, voices and testimonials. But section 8.1(i) prohibits advertisements that create “unnecessary demand” for medical procedures or promote “fear-based marketing”. Without objective criteria, such expressions leave considerable room for subjective interpretation and inconsistent enforcement.

Hospitals may publish factual details of services, charges, accreditation and doctors’ credentials. Yet Section 8.1(iii) restricts advertising professional achievements and success rates, and Section 8.1(v) prohibits promotional “before and after” surgical photographs, except for specified scientific or educational purposes. Such blanket restrictions risk regulatory overreach, particularly when authentic, appropriately contextualised images could help patients understand surgical outcomes. Section 9.2 also restricts the use of doctors’ photographs for self-promotion, including on letterheads and signboards. These restrictions apply only to registered medical practitioners under the NMC’s jurisdiction.

Patients rarely possess the same medical knowledge as those treating them. Even amid an abundance of AI-enabled health information, choosing a surgeon or assessing a hospital’s safety record remains difficult. Verifiable professional achievements, including the number of surgeries performed, years of experience and treatment outcomes, could help patients make informed choices. While such figures can be misleading without context, they are fundamentally different from unsubstantiated claims to be the “best” or to guarantee success, which the guidelines already prohibit. Rather than restricting genuine professional accomplishments, requiring their accurate and transparent disclosure could better serve patients’ right to informed choice. The answer may lie in better disclosure, rather than less information.

The guidelines seek to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, while Clause 8.1(ii) restricts promotion, suggesting commercialisation of medical practice. But in India, profit-making healthcare is lawful, as section 2(c) of the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, recognises privately operated hospitals, and section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, enables lawful commercial enterprises, including hospitals. Government policy also permits 100% FDI in hospitals.

Article 19(1)(g) protects citizens’ freedom to practise a profession or conduct business, subject to reasonable restrictions. In the case Tata Press v. MTNL (1995), the Supreme Court recognised commercial speech under Article 19(1)(a), including the public’s right to receive information, while permitting restrictions on misleading advertisements. The current guidelines appear to treat commercialisation itself as a problem, without clearly distinguishing legitimate business interests from practices that mislead or exploit patients.

Central and State government schemes undertaken in the larger public interest are exempted, and can advertise. Flexibility for vaccination drives and other health programmes is understandable. But the exemption is broad. Safeguards should remain equally important whether a campaign is run by the government or a private hospital. Patients seeking private healthcare may independently praise or criticise doctors. But the guidelines remain silent on hospitals and practitioners using unsolicited patient testimonials for promotion. What if a patient voluntarily posts an account and a hospital subsequently shares it? The distinction remains unresolved.

Graded penalties are intended for violators, starting with a warning and mandatory ethics training for the first violation, and increasing to a 6- to 12-month suspension for subsequent violations. At the same time, repeated offences could lead to removal from the register for one to three years. State Medical Councils will enforce these provisions after issuing show-cause notices and considering doctors’ explanations. Appeals can be made to the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board.

The guidelines remain unclear about who can initiate complaints and the evidence required. It addresses genuine concerns, but its broad and ambiguous provisions may create confusion over compliance and leave considerable room for subjective enforcement, particularly affecting smaller hospitals. Protecting patients from misleading advertisements and commercial exploitation is necessary. However, treating commercial intent itself as inherently suspect serves little purpose. Clearer distinctions between legitimate professional communication and unethical promotion would better serve both patients and healthcare providers.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.
